chapters.title: From the Florida House to Congress
chapters.dek: A state legislator became a nationally visible Trump ally.
chapters.body: Donalds served in the Florida House from 2016 through 2020 before entering Congress in January 2021 [[BD01, BD02, BD04, BD05]]. His federal identity is anchored by FEC candidate H2FL14186, while his later gubernatorial campaign is governed by Florida's separate campaign-finance system [[BD19, BD23]].

chapters.title: Immigration and Israel in the House record
chapters.dek: Recorded votes provide a firmer basis than broad ideological labels.
chapters.body: Donalds voted for the 2024 Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act and for the 2025 Laken Riley Act [[BD06, BD07]]. In an August 2026 interview he argued for legal immigration with assimilation while rejecting unauthorized immigration [[BD16]].

chapters.title: The 2026 Florida primary
chapters.dek: Trump's endorsement and a fragmented field shaped the contest with Fishback.
chapters.body: Trump publicly offered his endorsement before Donalds formally launched his gubernatorial campaign in February 2025 [[BD08, BD09, BD10]]. Fishback later attacked Donalds over corporate interests, while Donalds declined a challenger debate amid disputes over party forums [[BD11, BD13, BD14, BD15]]. Official results gave Donalds 47.79% of the Republican primary vote and Fishback 10.48% [[BD03]].

chapters.title: Money and the governing coalition
chapters.dek: Federal, state-candidate and state-committee records must remain separate.
chapters.body: Donalds's federal House committee, Florida gubernatorial account and Friends of Byron Donalds PAC are distinct entities and reporting buckets [[BD19, BD20, BD23]]. Reporting connected detention-industry donors to the state political committee, but a contribution alone does not establish a policy exchange [[BD18, BD22]].
